utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all, I would like to make sure that you are hearing the interpretation into your language of what I am saying; and if you can, please say that you have understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You have been called as a witness by the Defence. Before you give your solemn oath, I would like to hear your personal details. So please could you introduce yourself, tell us your particulars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fehim Muratovic, and I was born in Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch his date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Are you employed at the moment? What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm employed as an active professional soldier in the army of the federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your date of birth again because that is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 13th of June, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please -- you have just said that you work in a ministry of some sort.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness because it is overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a captain by rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you -- were you employed at the time? Were you in the army? If you were, where were you, in which military formation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not work in the army. I worked in a private enterprise, and I worked in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Did you ever testify before any state or international court about the events which took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time that you are testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I am testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will now show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now. Before I give the floor to the Defence I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we'll be following here this afternoon. This should enable you to answer the questions to the best of your ability. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by the Defence, and you have certainly already met a member of the Defence before you appeared here for your examination. The examination-in-chief should not take more than an hour and 45 minutes, but the questions put to you should be phrased in a neutral and non-leading manner. Once these questions have been put to you and you have answered those questions, the Prosecution, who are to your right, there are three members of the Prosecution, but only one of them will cross-examine you, the Prosecution will then conduct their cross-examination, and they will have the same amount of time as the Defence. After that stage, Defence counsel, who are to your left, may, if they believe that it is necessary, ask you additional questions which are related to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. There are two Defence teams since there are two accused. You will first be examined by one of the Defence teams and then, perhaps, by the other Defence team. At the end of these two stages, after the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination and the re-examination, the Judges who are before you may ask you questions if they believe it is necessary, either in order to clarify some of the answers you have provided to the parties or because they believe that it is in the interests of justice to hear what your position is or what your testimony is with regard to certain events referred to in the indictment. In the course of this hearing, the parties might also show you some documents. Usually these documents are of a military kind. This is done in order to ask you to comment on these documents. This is how we will be proceeding. I would also like to point out two other important issues. You have taken the solemn declaration. You have said that you will speak the truth, and as you are well aware, this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. excludes false testimony. False testimony is an offence that is punishable by this Tribunal. And secondly, I would like to point out that when a witness answers a question, if the witness believes that his answer may be used against him at a subsequent date, the witness may refuse to answer the question. In such a case, which is quite exceptional, and we have never had any such cases to date, in such a case the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question, but the witness is granted a form of immunity. This is a provision that is in force in order to ensure that the truth can be determined and that the witness can assist us in determining the truth. I should also like to point out that the proceedings that are followed here are adversarial and the proceedings are based on your oral testimony and on the written documents that are presented in the course of the hearing or on written documents that have already been presented, and this is why your testimony is so important. The Judges have no written documents that concern you, so your testimony is important. You have a monitor before you, and you will see that everything said in the courtroom is transcribed, and you can see the transcript on the monitor. The English transcript is also evidence. If you feel that a question is too complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Sometimes the parties may ask very complicated questions without realising that the witness might lose the thread of their thought. So ask the person putting a complicated to you to rephrase it. Generally speaking, this is the proceeding -- this is the procedure that we will be following here, and what I have just informed you of is information that I provide to all witnesses who appear here. We will also be having two 20 to 25-minute breaks. We have these breaks for technical reasons and also to give you the opportunity to have a rest, because as you will realise, if you have to continually answer questions, this can be very tiring, and this is why it's good for the witness to have a brief break. If you feel that there are any difficulties, please inform us of the fact. We're here to deal with any difficulties that may arise. I will now give the floor to the Defence counsel who will commence their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I put my questions, I would like to ask you to pay attention to one more thing. You and I speak the same language, and as soon as I put the question to you, you can reply immediately without any difficulties. However, my question and your answer are interpreted so that Their Honours and all sides in the courtroom could follow what you are saying. So that is why I would like to ask you to wait for a few moments and only then begin to answer my question. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, you probably did not understand a question fully which the Judge asked you, so you partially responded to it and that is why I would like to put additional questions to you. You said that in 1992, you worked in a private company in Sarajevo. When did you work in this company?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After April 1992, where did you go and what did you do until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, I returned from Sarajevo to Zenica, and I immediately -- the aggression against my country began immediately, and I joined the TO units in Zenica right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, how long were you in the TO, in the Territorial Defence, and after that did you join some other military formation?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately until August 1992, once the first units were formed. After that, I joined the municipal defence staff in Zenica, and that was the anti-sabotage unit, and I was there until March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I began to work in the 3rd Corps Command in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties there at the command?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps Command, I worked on security.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So now you have augmented the answer to the question put to you by the learned Judge. You probably did not receive a complete interpretation, so you only partially told us what you did in that period. I would like to ask you now about your education and where you acquired it.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: I have university degree. I have a law degree from the University of Sarajevo. I'm a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From March 1993, you said that you worked in the military security of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Mr. Ramiz Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, please, could you tell us briefly how your competences, tasks were regulated, the tasks of the military security. What rules governed this type of work?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The task and the competencies of the military security service was regulated by the rules of work as well as the rules of work of the military police as well as by orders of the superior command, and these rules and regulations were mostly taken over from the former Yugoslav People's Army, and they were applied in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, Mr. Muratovic, what duties were performed by the military security service?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The security service, briefly, is analogous to the state security service, namely the military security service carries out the state security service tasks. It's in the military forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in order to protect the institutions, the staffs, and the facilities where the military forces are prepared for their use in peacetime and in wartime. The security service also is used to protect all activities during the planning of the use of armed forces in peacetime and wartime, and also that service, the military security service, is used to protect the armed forces from the inside and from the outside from any eventual threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us what these activities are. Could you classify them in some way? What were the immediate tasks and responsibilities of the military security service that you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: That service of the 3rd Corps where I worked, its activity could be classified into three sections; counter-intelligence tasks, military police tasks, and staff security tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, could you please tell us whether the military security service had any kind of relationship vis-a-vis the military police of the 3rd Corps; and if it did, what kind of a relationship was that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The military security of the 3rd Corps of course had a relationship vis-a-vis the military police, the military police battalion of the 3rd Corps. It was an organ which commanded the military police. The military security is the expert organ through which the commander controls and commands the military police. The military security is entrusted with the proper use of the military police forces, and it plans all of its activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, could you please tell me, who were the military security organs immediately subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: These organs were subordinate -- well, let me explain this first, in which units these organs existed. The lowest ranking unit is a battalion. That's the lowest ranking formation. So from a battalion up through the battalion, division, corps, up to the Main Staff. We have dual responsibility. We have command and expert responsibilities. The chiefs of the security organs from the battalion up to the Main Staff are responsible to their immediate commanders. In the expert sense, from the battalion upwards, they are responsible to the security chiefs of the immediate superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Muratovic, if we were to qualify this line of command over the service, would we say that this was a unified command or would it be a dual line of command?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: It's a dual line of command. The command is dual. We have the command line, and we have the expert line. The command line, we have the immediate superior commander, and in the expert line we have the immediate chief of that security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the expert line of command, what was your duty in relation to the superior security command? Were you obliged to report to this command? Did you receive expert instructions from it which you had to comply with and so on?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as our duties were towards the superior command, we were obliged to report to the superior command. However, we were not obliged to report about the overall use of all the equipment and means of the service. If we look at the hierarchy in the army, the immediate control was in the hands of the minister of defence or the Commander-in-Chief, and they were the only ones who were supposed to know about all of the methods and the work of the security services. The other commanders in the lower-ranking units could be informed about the results of the application of the work and methods of the military security service but only to the extent that the authorised commander permitted this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, the things that you did in the military security service of the 3rd Corps, amongst those things, were you obliged -- did you -- were you allowed to talk about your expert methods and the intelligence on a daily basis to the corps commander, to report to him?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: We were not obliged to report to the corps commander regarding all of the applications of our expert methods and means of operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier that the service overall was commanded by the minister of defence and the supreme commander or Commander-in-Chief. Could you please tell me, could the commanders of lower-ranking units from the battalion up to the corps, which all had military security organs, could he or could they command the military security service as a whole?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: In the command sense, they could, but as far as the expert part was concerned, they were not able to do that. The expert part of our work, as I said, was something under the jurisdiction of the minister of defence or the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if the commander of a lower-ranking unit, of lower rank than the supreme commander or minister of defence, could such a commander monitor your intelligence information and your operational methods, and did he have any jurisdiction as far as counter-intelligence activities were concerned, which was also amongst the tasks of your service?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: No, they could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier that you had certain responsibilities and the commander, through the military security service, commanded over the military police. Could you please tell us how the military security service acted in relation to the military police. Could you please clarify that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The military security service conducted the work of the military police, issued them their tasks, and controlled the implementation of those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in view of the fact that you came there in March of 1993 to the military security service, what was the situation there? What was the personnel at the time in the military security service, and could you please tell us how it developed in the source of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the military security service of the corps, at the same time the chief of the military security service of the 3rd Corps also came, Mr. Dugalic. When Mr. Dugalic came to the command of the 3rd Corps -- before he came the military security service was just being developed. Practically, you could say that it didn't exist. In my view, there were few qualified personnel from the former JNA there because these are tasks which are reserved for people of different ethnicity than the one we belonged to. So there were few such officers who were able to organise the military security service in all units. Once Mr. Dugalic came, whose task this was in the former JNA, the military security service began to develop more rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your personal duties that you were working on in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: In the military security service of the 3rd Corps, there were establishment post of clerk and assistant chief of staff security and police affairs and counter-intelligence affairs. Once I came there, I was first given the task of a clerk, and then after that I became assistant commander of counter-intelligence as well as staff and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, could you please tell us, within these counter-intelligence duties, who did you consider as subjects or objects that were interesting for the needs of normal functioning of the army? Which foreign subjects were given your attention?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: We gave attention to all persons who in any way threatened the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Once I arrived to the military security service in March, in April there was the problem of small groups of foreign nationals of Asian origin who appeared in our area, and regardless of the fact that they were not members of the army, with their behaviour they influenced -- or they had an effect, a negative effect on the image of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that this happened, did that lead to certain orders and tasks for the military security service so that this element could be monitored and so that adequate measures could be taken in response to this?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Already in April we sent an inquiry to the administration of the security of the B and H army General Staff. We asked them what to do. We were powerless. We didn't know who these people were. We were unable to identify them. We didn't know how many people exactly were involved. So already in April we were slowly applying some operative measures in relation to these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, did you do this kind of work periodically or was this an ongoing task in the course of that year for the military security service?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: This was a priority task for the military security service that was ongoing. It was not something that was done periodically. Throughout 1993, we were continuously busy with this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier, Mr. Muratovic, that you didn't have the best personnel available, there weren't enough experts from that field who could have been given these tasks. Could you please tell us now, what were your material means at your disposal so that you could apply all the proper methods to monitor the enemy, including this Afro-Asian element that you mentioned that could have some kind of effect on the image of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As I said before, the army was just being developed, just like the service itself. We had very little personnel and even less technical means for any kind of more serious approach to resolve this problem, but the few means that we had at our disposal we did manage to implement certain measures in relation to these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about some of the methods that you used when dealing with certain groups; and could you use the same methods for the different groups?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: At the time in Zenica, there were about two groups. One called itself the Turkish guerilla, and the other one was the El Mujahedin group of foreigners. We tried to intercept some of their written communications to intercept some of their telephone conversations, and as far as the Turkish guerilla is concerned, we managed to infiltrate some of our men into that group or, rather, to develop an a network of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since -- given the procedure that you implemented from the end of April until the end of 1993, what I'm interested in is whether you informed your superior command the results of the information you obtained; and in certain areas could you take your own decisions independently or did you have to have the approval of your superior command?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as all the measures are concerned, as far as all the methods that we used are concerned, we reported to the superior command, and we also received specific tasks and instructions from them. We couldn't do anything on our own initiative if we hadn't received any specific orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just said that there was some sort of a guerilla group in the area, when did you manage to infiltrate your own men into that guerilla group? Was that at the beginning of the year or did you take certain measures at some other time?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: We took measures with regard to the Turkish guerilla towards April or May. We needed some time to gather information about that group. Once we had obtained the necessary information about the strength, about the command structure of that group, we then took certain measures. We arrested the entire leadership of the group, all the leaders of the group. Before that, we sent an inquiry to the General Staff in Sarajevo, asking what to do. We were told that they should be placed under the control of the ABiH or that they should be arrested. Since they didn't want to be placed under the ABiH control, we arrested the leaders of the group, and as of that time, they no longer existed as an organised group. The remainder of the men, who were Bosniaks from the surroundings, joined the regular ABiH units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you needed to work for a few months before you obtained information that you could forward to your superior command. A minute ago, you also mentioned that at some point in time in Zenica an El Mujahedin detachment arrived. In 1993, were you able to establish contact of any kind with that detachment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to interrupt you. You've just said that the headquarters of the El Mujahedin detachment -- he mentioned -- you said that he mentioned the headquarters of the El Mujahedin detachment. He hadn't mentioned it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My colleague has just said that on page 25, line 2, it says that the El Mujahedin was there with the headquarters and that's a mistake. I thought that's what the witness said. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the El Mujahedin detachment at any point in time have its headquarters in Zenica? And if that was the case, when?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The El Mujahedin detachment did have its headquarters in Zenica. That was -- well, I can't say when exactly -- in the second half of 1993. The third quarter of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell me, could you use these methods against them, the ones that you used against the guerilla group?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: We tried to do so, but the group was quite different when compared to the first Turkish guerilla group. This was a very hermetic group, and they would not allow anyone to approach them. We also intercepted some of their written communications. We tapped some of their phones, but we weren't able to establish a network of cooperation within that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, using all those methods up until the end of 1993, were you able to find out how many such men there were, where they were from, what their names were? Given all those methods and efforts that you made up until the end of 1993, did you find out anything that would have enabled you to assess their strength and their size?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: I personally worked in the security organ of the 3rd Corps, almost until the end of the war. Throughout the wartime period, I worked in that organ. And during that time we never found out anything about their numbers, their names, their origin, how they had arrived there, given that our territory had been completely blocked off. They would appear with cars with number plates from foreign countries, with Croatian number plates. We managed to identify some of them, a few of them, and they had passports from Western European countries. I personally saw some Danish passports, British passports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You as the security service, were you able to enter the territory where the El Mujahedin were located, and were you able to conduct investigations there as you were able to conduct investigations in any other army units?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, I personally never entered the premises, the territory or the premises of this group, nor did any of my colleagues manage to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given those problems, did all the security organs start cooperating in order to clarify certain incidents that the units -- that those units were involved in?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, towards the end of 1993, or perhaps at the beginning of 1994, a British citizen was killed in Zenica. Paul Godal. He was a humanitarian. I was part of a team that had been formed by the military security and the Zenica security and the state security service. Since we had certain indications on the identity of the perpetrator or, rather, we knew which car had been used when the crime was committed, when this car appeared in town again, five or six foreigners were arrested, and we managed to establish the identity of the murderer of this man. The case was processed by the civilian organs and by the courts, and he was sentenced to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about something entirely different. In the course of your duties that involved police work within the military security service, did you at any point in time receive the task to go to Bugojno; and if so, when did this happen and why did you go there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when the conflict in Bugojno ended in the second half of August 1993, my superior officer, Mr. Dugalic, ordered me and my colleague from the service to go to Bugojno and to take note of the situation up there. Since we knew that a number of HVO members had been arrested in Bugojno and the chief of security had previously been present in Bugojno, and since these were the policies of the 3rd Corps to move all those prisoners to the centre in Zenica, the prisoner centre in Zenica, we went to the site to see why these individuals were not being transferred to the prison centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you went to Bugojno, did you know how and why this conflict broke out? Was it a planned operation of the ABiH or the conflict in that time -- in that town, did the conflict in the town between the army and the ABiH arise in some different way?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information we had in the corps, and we didn't have complete information, although Zenica and Bugojno are not far from each other, at the time in 1993, Bugojno was too far from Zenica, and going to Bugojno from Zenica was an adventure at that time. It meant risking one's life. I've now forgotten what your question was. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether this operation in Bugojno was planned or do you know how this conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: According to the little information we had, and especially when I arrived there, I gained an idea of what had actually happened in Bugojno. Given what we heard in Bugojno, HVO members in Bugojno, in Vrbanja and the village of Bristovi established checkpoints. When army members saw that they established checkpoints there without having agreed on this with the ABiH, they established their own checkpoints in the vicinity of the HVO checkpoints. Soon afterwards, at one of the checkpoints, there was a skirmish, a clash. Two HVO members were killed. A Zenica commission was established to investigate the matter, and when negotiations were held with regard to the incident, HVO members arrested three members of the Bosniak negotiation team, and this is how the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that a large number of individuals were arrested, and when the chief went there, this is what he established. According to your information, were there any prisons in Bugojno in which all these individuals could be detained, and do you know where they were? Did you have any information on where they were initially held?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the conflict broke out suddenly, and on the Bosniak side, no one had planned that conflict. So we didn't have premises for prisoners in advance, but the War Presidency in Bugojno designated the primary school, the furniture salon, and a few other places, the sports hall and a few other places as places where these individuals could be detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the policies of the 3rd Corps Command with regard to POWs, and were there any orders from the 3rd Corps Command to that effect?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Command issued very strict orders. It stated that the Geneva Conventions should be strictly adhered to as far as the treatment of POWs was concerned. All the units in the territory of the 3rd Corps strictly adhered to those rules, and as far as I know, none of the Geneva Conventions, none of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions were violated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were those prisoners to be taken, according to the policies of the 3rd Corps Command, and where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The central place was the centre for POWs in Zenica, which was in the KP Dom in Zenica, which had existed there since the Austro-Hungarian times. That institution had been created for those purposes, and that building was secured by the 3rd Battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps. All the conditions existed there for the safe detention of detainees. It was possible to visit them. The International Red Cross could visit them, members of the clergy could visit them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bugojno, did you try to find out any information from your colleague about the matters you have just been discussing about the treatment of the prisoners, the arrested HVO members, and were the commander's orders fully obeyed?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Bugojno, we visited our colleague from the local unit, from the 307th Brigade, and naturally we asked about the situation in the centres that had been established for POWs. He mentioned an incident. He said that two members of the local unit of the 307th Brigade who were from the village of Vrbanja and whose entire families had been killed by HVO members, he said that these men entered the furniture salon and beat up a number of arrested HVO members. As a result of the beatings, one of these men died. We asked him what he had done about this. He arrested or imprisoned these individuals and instituted legal proceedings against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to what your colleague said about the 307th Brigade, did you inform the 3rd Corps Command of what he had told you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: When we returned from Bugojno, we drafted a written report and we informed our superior officer of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, did you at any point in time have any doubts about what your colleague had said; namely, that the perpetrators had been arrested and proceedings had been instituted against them?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never doubted what my colleague had told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of answers did you receive with regard to the necessity of transferring detainees to the prison centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Since we're talking about a large number of prisoners, approximately 400 people, at that point, in my opinion, it was an impossible operation to transfer in the wartime roads 400 people from Bugojno to Zenica safely. It was almost impossible. In order to transfer about 400 people, you would need about ten buses. The road from Bugojno to Zenica in several places was not passable by bus. It was only possible to go past there in special vehicles. It would perhaps have been possible also to have trucks do that, but as far as I know, a couple of the trucks were inoperative. So it was not possible to organise that. From my own aspect, the aspect of security, this was something that was not doable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Bugojno, did you find out about other proposals in Bugojno at the time regarding the safety of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: When we were in Bugojno at that time, a number of Croatian intellectuals from Bugojno started an initiative, or they asked that these prisoners remain where they are, to stay in Bugojno, because in their opinion there was no need for them to be transferred to Zenica at all. It was easier to handle all of those people in Bugojno than to transfer them to Zenica under those circumstances. And I was there and I could see that it was possible that each of those individuals could go home in the course of the day and they could take baths, clean themselves, change clothes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said later that you found out that -- I apologise, but my colleague is warning me that on pages 22 to 24, there is a question -- actually, it's on page 31, lines 20 to 24, that there is something that is unclear, so I will ask you about that again. You said that your colleague from the 307th Brigade informed you that some people broke into the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A couple of members of that brigade. You also mentioned who those people were. You said what had happened to them so that they reacted in this manner. Can you please repeat that part of the answer. Could you tell us again what your colleague told us, because obviously it was not precisely translated.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Two members of the 307th Brigade, meaning those whose complete families were killed by members of the HVO in the village of Vrbanja, broke into the furniture salon, and they beat up several members of the HVO. One of the members of the HVO succumbed as a result of that beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now it's clear. Could you please, since you found out that these trucks that were prepared, that were out of service and because of that it was not possible to transfer these people to Zenica, do you know if anyone did, and if they did, who decided that all of those prisoners be placed in a certain location?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know and from what my colleague in Bugojno told me, the War Presidency of the Bugojno municipality and probably the suggestions from the Croat intellectuals all together made the decision on the establishment of a POW centre in Bugojno which was set up on the Iskra soccer stadium in Bugojno, and this is where these people were put. They were not transferred to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, after your visit to Bugojno and after you talked with your colleagues, did you tour some other areas during that particular visit to your colleagues in subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: When I went to Bugojno, on that occasion I also visited a unit of the 17th Krajina Brigade in Travnik. This unit was running a prison which was in the barracks in the town of Travnik. And on that occasion, my colleague and myself visited prisoner Ivan or Ivica -- Ivan or Ivica Josipovic - I don't know his name exactly - who happened to be there. That individual, while under the influence of alcohol, came to the checkpoint of the 17th Krajina Brigade. He didn't know where he was, and he behaved in an insolent way. They tried to check his identification, he put up resistance, and then he sustained some injuries. Following medical treatment, this person was taken to the prison in Travnik. My colleague who was with me together on that Zenica-Bugojno road knew this person personally and he requested, he insisted that we visit him. We sent to see him. He didn't have any complaints at all to the way he was being treated in the prison. This was my first time in the Travnik prison, and I was surprised at the conditions in the prison. They were more than good. Other than Josipovic, there were two other persons in the prison. One person, whose last name was Bonic, he's a person who is under age, or 18 years old at the most, who was found to have in his possession an ear that had been cut off from a person. We found him in the cell. He was lying on the bunk and reading a book. He was not being abused or mistreated in anyway. There was another person there, a person whose surname was Baskarada. He was also lying on his bunk-bed in the cell, and he wasn't having any kind of trouble either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you interested in the way those three or any other people were being treated? Was it possible for them to communicate with the International Committee of the Red Cross or did they have any objections to the way the prison was being run?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: The detainees in Travnik and Bugojno had no complaints about the way they were being treated in prison. Members of the ICRC regularly visited these individuals, and my colleague from the 17th Krajina also showed us a document from the ICRC where they were commending the situation as it was, as they had found it in the Travnik prison following a check they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That person who had put up resistance at the checkpoint and who had sustained some injuries and then after that he was given medical treatment, did you try to find out whether your colleagues conducted an investigation of that incident? Because Josipovic did need medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I asked my colleagues what had happened and what he did regarding this matter regardless of the way Josipovic behaved, regardless of his insolent behaviour. These two police officers from the 17th Krajina Brigade were subjected to disciplinary sanctions because of their conduct, and they were punished because of their conduct by their commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's quarter to four. We'll resume at about ten past four, and then I will give the floor to the other Defence team, after which the Prosecution will start with their cross-examination. We will then resume at ten past four. Mr. Mundis, is there anything would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, if I could, Mr. President. Perhaps if I could do this in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness out the courtroom. Witness, you'll have a 20 or 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am cognisant of the time. Mr. President, we've raised this issue before. It concerns the adequacy of the Rule 65 ter summaries. As is clear from a review of this summary in light of the witness's testimony, this witness testified with respect to a number of very important issues to this trial that are not covered in this summary. In particular, he talked about counter-intelligence, monitoring the Mujahedin, monitoring the Turkish guerilla, the method of dealing with these groups, a number of issues that are not contained in this summary, nor were we notified about this as I have raised this issue before by our colleagues in terms of being prepared for this. We are not prepared, nor can we be prepared during the course of 20 to 25 minutes to cross-examine this witness on these very important issues. I have a couple of proposed ways of going forward. We can either respectfully ask for additional time to prepare for our cross-examination. Alternatively, we could move on to the next witness for direct and commence the cross of this witness tomorrow. At any rate, in light of this, I am certainly advising the Defence that we are likely to have a number of additional or new documents which we may need to show this witness during the course of our cross-examination. We will provide those, at least notice of those documents to the Defence as quickly as possible, but it is extremely likely that we will have a number of new documents to present to this witness with respect to those issues that were not covered in the 65 ter summary. My colleague Mr. Neuner will be doing the cross. He says he needs probably an hour at a minimum to prepare his cross-examination. We can either move on to the next witness or we're going to need an hour at a minimum to prepare to cross this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. Defence counsel. I do have the summary, and there are certain issues mentioned -- which were mentioned and which aren't contained in the summary, and there is another issue that wasn't mentioned. There was the issue of the Guca Gora monastery in the summary but nothing was said about that in the examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, so far what I wanted to say is that what this witness has said is in the summary. It is true that in this morning's conversation with this witness my information about his visit to Guca Gora were not correct, that is obvious, and for those reasons I could not cover that question with him. However, I worked late and perhaps I should have informed my colleagues at half past twelve that I was going to deal with different questions, because I found out that this witness knew something about the operative measures about which we talked about with yesterday's witness. This time it is a shortcoming of the Defence, and I accept that we can move to question the next witness and that my learned friends on the other side prepare to cross-examine this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Instead of telling the witness to wait, it would be best for him to come back. We'll say that we're now releasing him, in inverted commas, and he will come back tomorrow. Mr. Usher, could you please call the witness back into the courtroom. I've been told that the second witness should arrive around 4.00. That would be very convenient since we'll be resuming at about ten past four.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We could then resume at about 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I've asked you to return because certain procedural issues have been raised, and as a result the Prosecution will cross-examine you tomorrow. You will have to return tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. You may now leave, have a walk, but you should come back for the hearing at 9.00 tomorrow. Since you have taken the solemn declaration you are now a witness who is testifying in the interests of justice so you shouldn't see either of the parties. You shouldn't meet members of the Prosecution or Defence counsel in the meantime. You may now leave, enjoy the afternoon, and we will see you tomorrow. We will now have our break, and we will resume at about 4.25 or half past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are continuing with the hearing. Before the next witness comes in, I would like to ask the registrar to say something, who will give us a number of corrections now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Two corrections and one clarification. The first correction refers to Defence document DH1880, which has been admitted, and it's not DH8880. The second correction: DH1064 ID, and not 1604 ID. So these are the two corrections. Besides that, I would like to clarify the following: Prosecution Exhibit P724 contains two documents. One is an order with internal marking 226/93. And the second part of the document is an order bearing the internal marking 226/93. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would now like to ask the usher to bring in the witness. How much time do you think you will need for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than an hour, Mr. President, but now since you're asking, I think that Witness HD should not be called to the courtroom tomorrow. I don't think that that's realistic since we will continue to -- the testimony of Mr. Muratovic. I don't know how things will go with Mr. Zlotrg. We also have Ragib Hodzic also, so I think it would be a good idea to inform you today that Witness HD will not be appearing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all, I would like to be sure that you're hearing the interpretation of what I'm saying in your own language. If so, could you please tell me, "I hear you and I understand you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness by the Defence. Before giving the solemn oath, I would like you to introduce yourself. Tell us your first and last name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Edib Zlotrg, 21st of October, 1958, in Nova Bila, municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you employed? What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I worked in the Ministry of Internal Affairs as a crime technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993; were you working on some specific job; and if you were, what was that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was working in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It was a public security station Vitez, actually, where I was working, and I was working as a forensics technician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applies to 1992 and 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in this post until the outbreak of the conflict in Vitez, until the 16th of April, 1993, when I was arrested by members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And after 1993, after you were arrested, did you then move to some other job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, in late May I was in the 3rd Corps Command, working in the security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could you please tell us, did you ever testify before any state or international court before about the events in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time that you're appearing in such a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I testified here in The Hague on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when you testified here in The Hague, did you testify as a witness for the Prosecution or a witness for the Defence; and in which cases did you testify, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified as a Prosecution witness in the case -- in the Aleksovski case; Santic, Josipovic and Kupreskic case; the Cerkez case; and I don't know, perhaps there were some other cases, but I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. How many times have you been here before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is my fifth or sixth time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifth or sixth time. Very well. When you testified, did you ask for any protective measures or did you testify in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always testified in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to ask you to read the solemn oath for the fifth or sixth time. You probably know it by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. You may sit down. And as you know, you are familiar with these proceedings, I will just give you a couple of very brief clarifications. You will respond to questions from the Defence - you have already met with the Defence - and when they complete their questioning, then you will be responding to questions put by the Prosecution, who are to your right. They will be cross-examining you. After that, the Defence will have another opportunity to ask you questions. After that, the Trial Chamber members might be asking you questions, or in the course of your testimony, in case we need further clarification or if we believe that you did not touch upon any topics that we think you should have talked about and that these topics are important in the interests of justice, then we may also ask you questions. It can also happen that the parties to the left and to the right, in the course of your testimony, show you some documents and ask you to provide them with your opinion. I would like to draw your attention to two important things. You have said that you will speak the truth, so false testimony is out of the question. I don't need to go into detail about that. You are probably very familiar with your duties as a witness. Another thing: As part of our proceedings, when a witness in answering a question thinks that this answer could some day be used against him, that he could incriminate himself, in that case the witness could refuse to answer such a question. This has not happened to us in these proceedings, but if such a thing did happen, the Trial Chamber could tell the witness to answer this question but to extend some kind of immunity to him. All of this -- the objective of all of this is to establish the truth, that a witness who speaks the truth in answering the question is able to express himself freely. If the questions seem too complicated or complex, you can ask the person asking the question to rephrase them. As you know, we have breaks. We will have one break before the end of the hearing today. If the parties keep their promises regarding the time they require for your testimony, your testimony will be completed this evening. If it continues beyond that, then you will have to come back tomorrow. This is all that you need to know about the proceedings today. Now I'm giving the floor to the attorney who will be questioning you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zlotrg, I would like to ask you, once I put the question to you, to make a slight pause before you begin answering so that the interpreters could interpret everything that you are saying, so that the Trial Chamber and all the parties in the courtroom could follow your testimony. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you're a forensics expert. What were your duties on the 6th of April, 1992, when the JNA and the Serbian forces attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was working in the public security station in Vitez as a forensics expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, did you serve in the JNA and did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I was a reserve private.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in the public security station until the 16th of April. Why did your duty stop working as a public security station employee in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The rank is warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 16th of April there was a general attack by the HVO on Vitez, and since I was in the town, in my apartment, I was arrested in the apartment and taken to the cultural hall where my other friends and neighbours were also brought in. They were all of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until when were you held prisoner, and where were you held throughout your period of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was in the cultural centre for a few days. One evening, at about -- on or about the 27th or 28th of April, military policemen appeared and they took us away. They took four or five of us from the cultural centre away, and from other places where they were detaining Bosniaks. We were taken to dig trenches. And instead of going to dig trenches that evening, we went ended up in a prison in Kaonik and on the following day we were taken to dig trenches. When an exchange had been agreed on an all-for-all basis, the 13 of us were placed in the chess club premises, and when UNPROFOR members found us, we were transferred to the Kaonik prison, probably to conceal us. On the 16th of May -- this is what they did when -- when the UNPROFOR found our traces. On the 15th of May, our exchange was agreed on, and on the 16th, 16 Bosniaks were exchanged. That was the first exchange between the army and the HVO in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that after the exchange in the second half of May you became a member of the 3rd Corps Command. You were in the military security service. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. A few days after the exchange, I became a member of the military security service in the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You used to work in the civilian police and later in the military security service. Mr. Zlotrg, could you briefly tell us what sort of tasks the military security service was involved in.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to. In November 1993, I was demobilised. I returned to the place. A lot of time has passed since then, but on the whole the military security service and the state security service in the armed forces was involved in the protection of staffs, commands, institutions, buildings used by the armed forces to prepare the armed forces. So all these tasks involved security for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The work in the security service of the 3rd Corps, while you were there was it divided into certain fields, certain areas; and if so, which areas was the security service of the 3rd Corps involved in?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps security service was mainly involved in counter-intelligence, providing staff security and carrying out military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just mentioned the tasks of the military police, tell me, what was the attitude of the military security service towards the 3rd Corps military police battalion? What was the relation between the two?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: On the whole they would supervise them or, rather, help them to train. They would assess military policemen and, naturally, were also responsible for the work of the military police and the way in which MP units were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, tell me, who was your immediate superior officer in the military security service of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Ramiz Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the service directly accountable to?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The service was directly accountable to the Ministry of the Interior and the Supreme Commander and to the command of the 3rd Corps, if the superior officer thought it was necessary to inform this person of the tasks carried out by the security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given your answer, or in light of your answer, could you provide me some clarifications. Did the military security service have just one line of command or a number of chains of command?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, there were two chains of command. One was based on command responsibility and the other was based on security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, but who was, in the end, in charge of the entire security service given this dual chain of command? Did this dual chain of command go right up to the top or was this chain of command united at some point?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, there was the Ministry of Defence and the Supreme Commander. These were the individuals who had final authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of right did a commander of a lower unit, a battalion or a brigade or a corps, have to know about your work?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Only if the superior officer from the military security service thought that it would be appropriate to provide a subordinate unit with information only in such cases did a subordinate unit have such authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any fields of work that a commander of a lower unit could not be made familiar with without your approval? Were there any -- was there any information, any methods, et cetera, that were planned within the service as a professional organ from the bottom to the top? Perhaps I haven't been sufficiently clear. You said there were a number of fields, counter-intelligence, policework, et cetera. Were there any fields in which a commander of a lower unit -- to which a commander of a lower unit had no access?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, that was the counter-intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the relation -- what was the attitude of your military security service towards the organs of military security in subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We assisted members of the security services in subordinate units. We supervised them. They reported to their superiors. They were accountable to their superiors, and they were accountable to the chief of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What fields were you engaged in on the whole while you were in the security service in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Since I came from the police, I spent most of my time working on military police matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, what sort of policies did the 3rd Corps pursue with regard to prosecuting individuals who had committed crimes? Was the position of the 3rd Corps clear with regard to how you in the security service should treat perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They had a clear position: All perpetrators of crimes had to be punished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago you said that for a certain period of time you were a prisoner and now you have just said that you were involved in military police matters. While you were involved in such work, did you ever think that while working with prisoners or others you were perhaps treating them in a way that was vengeful or were you acting in accordance with orders that had been issued?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, I never found myself in such a situation. I'd been through such a calvary myself, and I lost my brother and his wife in these events, and I wouldn't want anyone to suffer the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to prisoners of war held by the ABiH, was it quite clear to you in the security service -- were you quite clear about the policies of the 3rd Corps and the policies of its commander as far as the treatment of POWs was concerned?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. We were to respect the Geneva Conventions and abide by the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As part of those policies, did the 3rd Corps have certain premises where POWs could be kept? If prisoners were captured in the course of combat, was it known where they should be taken, and if there was such prisoners sent to institution, where was it and what was it like?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. There was a centre for POWs in Zenica on the premises of the Zenica KP Dom, the Zenica penal and correctional facility. The position was that the Geneva Conventions should be respected. As I had been in prison, as I had been in an HVO prison, and since I had worked with the detained HVO members, I can tell you that I received food in Busovaca once a day. It was insipid food, and as a member of the command, I would also eat stale bread. But when I went to the KP Dom premises, they had electricity there. They had a TV. They had three meals a day. I didn't have any electricity in my flat; they had electricity around the clock. They had an area where they could go out for a walk, so they had the conditions for a normal life. It was as if they were staying in a hotel if compared to the premises I was kept in when I was in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zlotrg, please tell me whether you received complaints from international organisations or the ICRC. Did you receive any complaints about the treatment of the prisoners held by the army in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. On the contrary; they were always content.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you whether in the course of your duties in the military security service you received the task of going to Bugojno. If you did, why did you go there and when did you go there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I was given the task of going to Bugojno after the clash between the HVO and the ABiH. Prior to that, Dugalic had been in Bugojno, and we were assigned the task of going to see how his orders were being implemented, the orders that he had issued when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you went to Bugojno or while you were there, did you receive any information on the cause of the conflict in Bugojno? Was this a planned military operation of the ABiH or did this conflict break out in some other way? Did you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Before I went to Bugojno, we had some information but only the information that we had received through regular reports that the assistant commanders for military security and units had sent to the 3rd Corps Command. Upon arriving in Bugojno, since I have quite a lot of relatives there, I spoke to them and everything fitted in. The conflict broke out in a place called Vrbanja after HVO members had set up a checkpoint. On that occasion, they captured three policemen, if I'm not mistaken, and a couple of army members. Then later on, the ABiH established a checkpoint a little further down below and an incident broke out and that's how the ball started rolling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, before you arrived in Bugojno, or when you arrived there, was there a prison where individuals who had been arrested in the course of the conflict could be held or, rather, do you know where these individuals were held?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: There wasn't a prison there. There were a number of buildings which were appropriate for the accommodation of a large number of people at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, did you receive any information as to who had designated those buildings or the governor -- or who had designated a governor for those premises where those individuals were kept?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke to the assistant commander of the Donji Vakuf brigade, I think it's the 307th, Mr. Handzic. We also spoke to the assistant commander for security of the Operations Group, and they told us that the War Presidency of the Bugojno municipality had designated these buildings and appointed governors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you said earlier on that there was a centre for POWs in Zenica, tell me whether your colleagues to whom you spoke, the colleagues you just mentioned, told you anything about how they intended to transfer those arrested individuals to the centre in Zenica. Did the technical and security conditions exist for such a transfer?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke about this, and they said that they tried to organise a convoy. However, the vehicles were faulty, so they had to postpone this. While we were up there, this was supposed to be carried out, this transfer was supposed to take place. But I think that it was technically impossible to organise a convoy of prisoners and send it to Zenica, because a number of sections of the road were under sniper fire and in the range of the artillery. So the consequences of such a transfer could have been quite negative.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would now like to show a number of documents to the witness when I ask -- when I put some new questions to the witness. Could these documents be distributed to my colleagues in the courtroom, to the Chamber, and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, could you please look at the document that is under tab 4. It's 1391 on the document. That's the number. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is an information from the 17th of August, 1993. Do you have information that your service received, information that it was not possible to transfer the prisoners to Zenica for the reasons which are given in this information?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: At the time we were out in the field, and on the 17th of August we happened to be in Bugojno, and that's when Mr. Dzafic told us that it was not possible to transfer the prisoners. And we told him that only those persons who had been charged, about whom there were indications that they had committed a criminal act and who were supposed to held responsible for that, and I think this is perhaps about 20 or 25 people that were in this category. When we were there, we found out that the War Presidency had already found a place to accommodate the rest of the prisoners - this was the area just below the Iskra stadium - and that they were already in the process of negotiations with the Croatian Defence Council to exchange these individuals, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, earlier you were talking about the causes of the conflict about which you had certain information that you found out about when you came to Bugojno. Could you please look at documents under numbers 1 and 2. Under 1 is a document 1320, and this is a document by the 317th Brigade. And document DH1319, which was sent to the command of the 3rd Corps. So could you please tell me whether these documents in fact reflect the information that you received in that period about the causes of the conflict in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. This is mostly the same as the things that we found out while we were in that area, in the area of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, since you also met with the assistant security commander of the OG and the 307th, were you trying to find out what their -- how these prisoners were being treated and whether there were any incidents?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: One of our tasks was also to see how the prisoners of war were being treated. We also know that our chief, Mr. Dugalic, instructed that the Geneva Conventions be strictly adhered to, including how they should treat the prisoners of war. So the assistant commander of the 307th Brigade informed us that there was an incident in which two members of the army entered certain premises and beat up six members of the HVO, one of whom succumbed as a result, unfortunately. He also informed us that those two persons were arrested and that they were being charged, that they had been charged for their actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you worked in the military security service, was this the proper way in which the military unit -- military police unit was supposed to react at the point in time when its members committed some kind of impermissible act or a criminal act in particular?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. They acted in accordance with the law and their competencies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time have any doubts about what the assistant commander for security told you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, we did not. There was no reason for us to doubt anything that he said. He could have not told us anything at all about it, but he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at the document under number 3. That's DH63 ID. A little earlier you said that you knew that the War Presidency appointed a temporary administrator for these temporary facilities where the prisoners of war were located. Could you please tell me whether this is a document which in fact confirms what you found out from the colleagues whom you met in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, that is it. We found out that the War Presidency formed these -- or established these areas to keep HVO members in detention and that they appointed an administrator.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at document under number 6, document number DH176 ID. It's a little bit difficult to see. Are you able to read this document? This is a decision of the War Presidency, setting up the Iskra stadium as a temporary detention facility of civilian and military persons. Could you please tell me whether this decision coincides with the information that you got in Bugojno that the War Presidency was looking for a way to place all these prisoners in one place.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier that on the 17th and the 18th we were in Bugojno, and that's when we were informed that the War Presidency had found a place to locate these prisoners, and this document indicates that this was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 4 of this decision. Can you read it, please, if you're able to see it properly.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It states that this decision goes into effect on the day of its adoption and the Executive Council of the municipality of Bugojno, the command of the 307th Motorised Brigade, and the command of the staff of the defence of Bugojno are responsible for the implementation of this decision. Is that what it states?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether it is customary that the War Presidency issues tasks to units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: At the time, the War Presidency was the main logistics body for the armed forces, so the War Presidency of the Bugojno municipality supplied all the units with all the materiel and equipment they required, and they probably took it upon themselves, felt it was their right since they were financing them also to issue decisions such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, could you please tell me, since you worked in a security organ, how much influence and what were your options as far as control of events in Bugojno is concerned. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I've already said before that it was very risky to go to Bugojno at all, because there was only one possible road for Bugojno, and on several sections it was under constant sniper fire, and on several places was within range of artillery. So when you set out to Bugojno, you never knew if you would reach it alive and if you would reach it at all. That was one of the difficulties. The other thing is the army did not have enough fuel to pull out the wounded, never mind fuel to send people to Bugojno. We were in touch with them and knew what was happening there only through our means of communications and through reports which the security organs there sent to the superior command, and that was something that the command of the 3rd Corps had access to. It took 24 hours to travel to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, you said that your colleague informed you about what happened in one case.
