Could you please tell us where this incident took place and whether these measures -- whether you were informed about these measures and whether you in turn informed your command about those measures.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Which incident are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about when you were talking about the Geneva Conventions. Didn't your colleague inform you about an incident that took place?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I already said that. He informed us also about the measures they took to punish the perpetrators. When we came back to the command, we made an Official Note and passed it up to the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at document under number 5. That's the command of the 3rd Corps, security sector, dated the 18th of August, 1993. Could you please look at this document. At the end, in the copy that I provided for you, it is not signed, but could you please tell me, do you recognise this document? It's document 1392. Could you please tell me, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report that my colleague Muratovic and I drafted after we returned from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of this document, does it -- is there a description of what happened in Bugojno, and doesn't it state what you found out there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Zlotrg, during that visit on that day, did you visit any other detention facility?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes; the one in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk with when you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We went there to arrest Ivan Josipovic. This is a person that I know very well. That same person worked in the regional police of the Croatian Defence Council during the conflict, and he's the brother of Vladimir Santic's wife, who, according to the information we had at the time, commanded the unit that attacked Ahmici. And for that reason, Josipovic was of interest to us. We wanted to see what his role was in the attack on Ahmici, because several units of the military police took part in the attack. And we also wanted to find out more about the role of Vladimir Santic in all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, when you saw Mr. Josipovic, did he complain to you about the way he was being treated in the detention of the 17th Krajina Brigade, and did you find out how he ended up being there at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: He did not complain. It was obvious that he had been physically mistreated, but all of that happened during the arrest itself, because he had gotten drunk in Busovaca and passed all the checkpoints and ended up at a checkpoint of the B and H army near Travnik. Since he was in the regional police crimes department, he was some kind of superior there, and he thought that this was an HVO checkpoint, he resisted arrest. And during the arrest, he sustained several blows. When he was arrested, the members of the military police there did not abuse him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me that at that time when you were talking to the military police members, did you receive any information about whether there was an investigation about that incident at the checkpoint and whether they found any grounds to prosecute the military police there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about the assistant security commander of the Krajina Brigade, Mr. Grudic, and we told him that the Geneva Conventions had to be respected. We used to draw attention to this and that it was necessary to treat the prisoners humanely any time we made any such visits. This person informed us about the circumstances of the arrest, and he informed us that the two police officers who had taken part in the physical abuse - actually, it wasn't a question of abuse, it was a question of using excessive force during arrest - that these people had been -- these two individuals had been charged for their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, could you please tell us whether you toured that facility and what the conditions were in that detention location.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. We went around it. We found two other persons from Vitez there. They didn't have any complaints about they were being -- about how they were being treated there either by members of the military police, although during the arrest of one of those persons an ear that had been cut off was found on that person, a human ear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking to members of the 17th Krajina Brigade, did you find out whether the ICRC had access to this detention facility and whether they had any complaints to make regarding the conduct towards the prisoners who were there?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. Grudic informed us that the ICRC had access to that facility, and he even said that they had been -- they had received some kind of commendation from the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This visit of yours, did you make a report about it to your superior commander?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: The report of the 18th of August also touches upon that visit to the Travnik prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zlotrg.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before the break, does the other Defence team have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it would be best to have our break now, and we will resume at about ten to six. The Prosecution will then have about one hour to cross-examine the witness, and then the Defence will be able to re-examine the witness. We'll now adjourn, and we will resume at ten to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume, and I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Forgive me for not calling your name. I've been practicing how to call it for days now and I still haven't got it right. So I would want to refer to you as "sir," if you don't mind. Thank you. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and together with my colleague we represent the Prosecution, as the President indicated to you earlier on. My role here is to clarify certain things that came out of your direct examination, and while doing so, if at any time you wish me to repeat a question or to rephrase a question, feel free. Do not hesitate, and I will oblige. Now, you told us that you became a member of the security department in -- sometime in mid-May of 1993. Could you tell us for how long your tenure lasted, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I was demobilised from the army when General Hadzihasanovic ceased to be the corps commander. That was in November 1993. And I returned to the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that would be for some mere six months, I take it. Could you tell us what position you held in the security department.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: As there were four or five of us in the military security service at the time, we dealt with all matters, but most of my work related to military police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time during that period while you were in the security department, did you also have another role? Did you perform a dual role?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. From the very beginning until I left, I worked in the military security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At any time at all, were you ever involved in the exchanges of POWs on behalf of the ABi 3rd Corps -- ABiH 3rd Corps? Were you ever a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I organised an exchange, but not as a liaison officer. I was assigned this task by my chief. I was assigned the task of getting the family of the president of the Vitez War Presidency out of Vitez, and that was the only occasion on which I was involved in an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In readiness for your position with the security department, did you receive any training?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive any training, because I had previously been in the police force, and the chief at the time probably had confidence in me given the work I had done in the police. But I must say that at the time of Yugoslavia, I was in the reserve force of the state security for a certain period of time. So it was probably on the basis of that experience that I had that he engaged me as a member of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, did you have to perform interviews with respect to detainees in the respective detention centres?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: On the whole, I would interview detainees in the centre for POWs in Zenica, and I can tell you that there was someone from the security service in the centre every day and controlled the way that members of the military police were treating the prisoners. I can also point out that it was possible for families to visit the prisoners, and it was also possible for the Red Cross to visit, as well as members of the peace mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, could you tell us the name of the centre in Travnik that you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. I was talking about the centre for POWs in Zenica. I was talking about this prison, and I said that we would supervise the battalion of the military police there on a daily basis, because they were in the town where the command of the corps was located. And a minute ago I also said that communications were difficult because parts of the road used to get to Travnik were under constant sniper fire. So I was only in Travnik on one occasion, and I compiled a report on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to understand you correctly, you only conducted interviews once during your tenure in the security department, and that would have been in Zenica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. I was in Zenica on a number of occasions, but every day someone from the security service was in the centre for POWs. But I was in Travnik only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I got it right now. Thanks. You mentioned awhile ago of the IRC, International Red Cross, and in your examination-in-chief, you indicated to my learned friend that Mr. Grudic informed you that the Red Cross was indeed very happy with the situation in the detention centre, or in the prison. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. The person was Grudic, and if I'm not mistaken, I think there's a written document in which the satisfaction of the International Red Cross is expressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But you yourself had not had this confirmation directly from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. As I have said, Grudic told the two of us about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With respect to the situation in Bugojno, prior to your going to Bugojno, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you had received reports on what was happening in Bugojno and the atmosphere, the general atmosphere in Bugojno. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the chain of command, assistant commanders for security had to provide information to their units about the situation in the zone of responsibility and information on the security. They had to provide such information to the 3rd Corps chief of security. This is what took place within security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Bugojno yourself, could you give us an idea of what the atmosphere was like when you went there yourself.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we went to see the assistant commanders. I have already mentioned this, but I can repeat it if necessary. I have family members who left Donji Vakuf and went to Bugojno. My uncle received a house from a Croat who remained in Bugojno, and they would visit each other. He also received a plot of land that he could till while he was a refugee. So if a man was a man, he remained a man, and if anyone was afraid of being punished, he would leave. Everyone was free to circulate. No one caused any trouble apart from those who had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You testified that, as far as you are aware, that there were no reports of any mistreatment of POWs in Bugojno. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. I said that we spoke to the assistant commander for security, Mr. Handzic, and he informed us of an incident when two army members broke into premises where HVO members were detained. On that occasion, they beat up six individuals, one of whom died. The others were treated and they were in hospital. He identified the perpetrators of this crime and proceedings had been instituted against them and a criminal report was going to be filed against them on the basis of the seriousness of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think we misunderstood some question somewhere along the line. My question is this: As far as you are aware, were there any complaints by any of the POWs with respect to mistreatment in the Bugojno centres?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We did not speak to the prisoners. We went there primarily to see how the army members were conducting themselves. We also visited the command, the command of the 307th Brigade and the command of the OG, where we told assistant commanders for security to comply with what the general had requested, namely that the Geneva Conventions should be respected and that prisoners should be treated humanely. When we spoke to them, Mr. Handzic informed us of the incident I have mentioned, and we told him to continue working like that and said that he had acted correctly when he arrested two army members. But we didn't have enough time to see or visit the premises where HVO members were being kept, because, as I have said, there were very few of us in the security service and we had to return. Before that we had spent a long period of time in Travnik. We only had limited time available, and we had to return to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying, then, that you could not really assist this Trial Chamber as to the conditions of the detention centres in Bugojno nor as to the treatment meted out to the POWs in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It depends on how you look at these things. I believe that the fact that we went there, the fact that the commander and the chief of the security service insisted on us seeing how the measures were being implemented, I think that this shows what the attitude of the superior command was towards POWs. But you must understand that there were a lot of duties that five men had to carry out in that zone of responsibility, in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. So we couldn't do everything. And secondly, we knew that these facilities had been visited by UNPROFOR members. If we had visited these buildings and if we had written anything, well, people would have had more confidence in UNPROFOR than in us. And we were more or less familiar with the situation in the facilities, because army members were present when UNPROFOR visited. Our main task was to point out to assistant commanders for security once again that they should strictly adhere to the Geneva Conventions. And finally, as I went through this tortuous experience and I know -- and I knew that the war would come to an end at some time, I knew that everyone would be held to account for crimes committed. Since this was the case, I tried to ensure that the assistant commanders for security didn't allow our men to do the same things that HVO members and members of the Republika Srpska army had done. I didn't want us to be identified with them. I'd been selected for execution. Fortunately, I remained alive. And I personally would not want someone to say that I had been a member of the army involved in genocide and crimes. This is how I always acted, on the basis of these principles, and I was assisted by my commander to a great extent since he insisted on respect for the Geneva Conventions, and I'm grateful to him for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that, but the question was very specific, and I'm going to ask you again. It could be just a yes or no answer. My question to you was you personally could not give an account as to the conditions of the detention centres in Bugojno nor as to the mistreatment of POWs in Bugojno having not been to the site yourself, as you said.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't on the site itself, but as I have said, we said that any irregularities should be punished, and the assistant commander had informed us of the fact that two individuals who had committed this unfortunate crime had been arrested. I didn't feel that it was necessary to check the allegations of the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So the point I'm making now, I'm suggesting to you that you couldn't see that people weren't maltreated. Neither can you say that the detention centres weren't up to par or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I didn't see it, but I did talk to this Croat who at no time said that he had been mistreated or that anybody else who was in his immediate vicinity was abused either.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, you spoke to somebody in Travnik. You visited Ivan or Ivica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I did see Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell me, when you visited in Travnik, was Mr. Josipovic the only person that you interviewed or you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. I've already said that there was this boy who was 17 or 18 years old, Bonic, on whom they found a human ear in his combat kit. There was another person also from Vitez. And I've already said that neither of them complained. Quite to the contrary; when we entered the detention unit, he was lying down, reading a book or a magazine, I don't remember. In detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You see, I asked you the question because it wasn't clear to me whether in fact you had just seen him there or you had spoken to him. That's why I asked if Mr. Josipovic was the only person you had interviewed. The impression I got at first is that you had just seen the young lad lying there, and now I think for the record you've said that you spoke to him. So my question to you now that you were at that centre: Were those three people the only people that you spoke to? And were these three people the only three people in the detention centre that day?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I only spoke to those three on that day, and I didn't see anyone else. I cannot state that they were the only three ones there, but I did only see the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you get an opportunity to see the conditions at the prison that day?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Since I said that I was in the prison, I will make a comparison. In Zenica it was an A-category hotel, and in Travnik it was B-category hotel. It was like that, compared to the conditions which were prevailing when I was at Kaonik. If I can just be --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a second. It will be unfair for you to say an A category and a B category because I think we don't know what you're referring to when you say A category and B category. But certainly in interests of time I don't want you to go into the comparison. I want you to tell me what were the conditions at that prison that you had seen on that day.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: When I mentioned the A category and B category hotel, what I meant was that 13 of us slept on a wooden platform which was two metres by three metres. This was in Busovaca at Kaonik. Here, however, everybody had their own bunk with a mattress and blankets. They had -- well, it was summer, so I can't really talk about the temperature in the room, but they had the full comfort that a person can enjoy in prison. They had three meals [Realtime transcript read in error "means"] a day, they had their own bunkbeds, they had an area to walk in. In Kaonik, we only had this two-by-three space to walk around in in the cell. That's where we allocated the space that we could walk around in. That was my comparison.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You weren't happy about being arrested and detained by the HVO, were you?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Well, I would like to see the person who would be happy when they were abused and detained. I would really like to see a person who would be happy to go through that and a person who wouldn't know if they would be alive by morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That is precisely my point and hence I do not want you to compare. I want you to tell me, based on the Geneva Conventions, if you think that the prison that you saw in Travnik, if it was -- if it stood up to the requirements of the Geneva Conventions. I don't want you to compare, because I know that you were unhappy in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: They had the same conditions that any prisoner would have today in any regular prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like a correction in the transcript. Page 75 -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the counsel very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that they had meals, and instead of "meals" in the transcript it says "means." So I would like to have that corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will take this into account and the correction has now been corrected at line 2, page 72. You may continue now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I am not sure if we got the final answer. You said that the conditions that any prisoner would have had today in any regular prison. Now, what does that mean? Does it mean that the conditions complied with the requirements under the Geneva Conventions? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I said that the conditions, according to the Geneva Conventions, were proper. They had as much freedom as civilian prisoners have today in slightly better prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated awhile ago to the Trial Chamber that your role was basically that of the military police-type of role, the task you undertook. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could I ask you what of security? Were you involved in security in any way?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: When I spoke about the security sector's role, I said that the security sector worked on counter-intelligence, staff, and military police tasks. So all of that was part of our work. This is only one segment of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do -- are you aware, then, during your tenure of any problems with respect to foreigners?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this question exceeds the framework of the examination-in-chief for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time during your tenure that your chief of staff or the commander of the 3rd Corps indicated that he was having a problem with foreigners? Did there come a time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Ms. Benjamin. The Defence did not ask any questions about foreigners. Your cross-examination, in accordance with the rules, must arise out of the content of the examination-in-chief, and we know that the Defence did not ask any questions about foreigners, Mujahedin. So why do you wish to question this witness about that? Of course the Chamber may permit you to put questions on that topic if this is in the interest of justice, however, we will make a decision on this. But before that, you need to explain to us why you are putting these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness, in examination-in-chief and again in cross-examination, said that he was involved in security matters. He was involved in it, and that, to me, arises out of security and security matters, because in fact most -- most of the documents that arise out of security, coming out of the -- of the security department had to deal basically with that area. Hence the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in his testimony the witness clearly stated that from mid-May until early November, he worked in the security service and that he personally worked on those tasks relating to military police tasks. Already the previous question to which I reacted he replied to my learned friend that he did not have anything to do with any matters relating to foreigners. So how can he expect it -- how can he be expected to respond to questions like that if he didn't deal with this matter in his work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has consulted, and we believe that there is no point in putting these questions. So the objection by the Defence is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Thank you, Mr. President. Well, I think we would have covered all the areas by the examination-in-chief and -- could you hold a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies, but I think there might be one more question from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, in your cross-examination and in your examination-in-chief, you indicated to me that your tenure came to an end somewhere in November when you were demobilised. Am I correct? And I think that's around the same time that the commander of the 3rd Corps had ceased being a commander. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes. I was demobilised, and Commander Alagic signed that document when he assumed duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And perhaps, sir, could you tell us if there was any connection with your demobilisation and the fact that the commander had no longer been corps commander? Is there any connection of any sort?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No. If you would like, I can explain to you why I asked to be discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: That won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there are no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am concerned, I have a few questions that I would like to put to you, a few brief questions, but I would like to hear your answers to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to the precise questions put to you by the Defence, you said that there was a sort of dual chain of command as far as military security is concerned. You said there was a chain of command including the 3rd Corps Commander, but there was also a chain of command which passed through the Ministry of Defence and the chief of the Main Staff. Could you explain to the Judges who was in fact your superior? Although you said it was Ramiz Dugalic, we would like to know who -- who was above him? Who was the real superior officer? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: On the basis of the chain of command, it was the 3rd Corps Commander, but in terms of the security service, it was the chief of the security service in the Main Staff, and he was directly accountable to the minister of defence and to the Supreme Commander, because the 3rd Corps Commander could be involved in a security service. He could be the topic of interest for the security service. So there was the chain of command, and there was the chain of command in the security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have clarified the answers that you provided to the Defence. Please have a look at the documents shown to you by the Defence, the report of the 18th of August; 1392. Do you have the document before you which is a typed three-page report, a three-page report. I can see that it's addressed to the 3rd Corps Commander. My questions have to do with this document alone. In the B/C/S version, the document that you have before you, I can see that on page 2 and 3, paragraphs were underlined, paragraphs that concern the conditions of detention for prisoners in the military prison in Travnik. That's on page 2. And on page 3, the fact that Mr. Handzic mentioned a problem with two soldiers who maltreated six HVO soldiers is also underlined. As far as you know, in your opinion, who underlined these sections? Was it Dugalic or was it someone at the level of the 3rd Corps who wanted to draw attention to these two elements?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I don't know who underlined that, because I am seeing this report of mine for the first time now. Well, I saw it when it was being compiled. Since Mr. Dugalic at the time when we were doing our task, he was ill. He wasn't working. So we were heading it as attention of commander. So I don't know whether it was signed by Hadzihasanovic or one of his commanders. I really couldn't say. But we sent it, Mr. Muratovic and myself, off without it being signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we have a look at this document, you've described -- you describe in detail your entire day, and it says that you visited the 306th command, and then we can see that you arrived in Travnik at 10.00 and you met Grudic, the assistant commander, et cetera. But on page 1, you say that you explained to Grudic the reasons for your visit. And in particular, as far as I can see in the document, the investigation into Josipovic. And when we continue to read further on, we can see that you interviewed him or interrogated him about Ahmici. Did you meet Mr. Josipovic to talk about the detention conditions or to interrogate him about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: We received the communication stating that Mr. Josipovic had been arrested. Since I knew Josipovic very well because we worked together for a while at the public security station in Vitez where he was the chief for administrative and legal affairs and because of some criminal acts he left the police force, basically he moved to the floor above us. He moved to the military police of the Croatian Defence Council, and his immediate superior was Pasko Ljubicic. I, however, happen to know that the wife of his -- of her -- the husband of his sister was commanding some of the units that participated in the attack on the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what I would like to know is, when he was interviewed, did this have to do with the detention conditions or was the purpose of the interview to obtain information on what had happened in Vitez and in Ahmici? What was the main objective of your interview with Josipovic? It's been written down, but I would like to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I tried to explain that. The main task -- the main objective was to find out as many particulars as possible about the crime in Ahmici. And then when we arrived, then we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that, in response to a question put to you by the Defence, you said that in the military security service you had two functions; surveillance of the military police, training the military police, and assessing their work. These were the three main areas in which you worked. Was interviewing part of your tasks? Perhaps that was the case, perhaps not, but I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: It all depended on our assessment. If we felt that for the purposes of acquiring precise and better information, then in each case we were obliged to join and assist the military police or any other security officers during the inquiry. We had assistance, that kind of monitoring, but we were also there to supervise them in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution asked you a minute ago when you were in Bugojno you met other members of the military, and you came to the conclusion that everything was proceeding very well. Wouldn't it have been necessary -- and this is something that anyone might wonder: Wouldn't it be -- wouldn't it have been necessary to see the detainees to make sure that everything was fine? In Travnik you saw these three detainees, but in Bugojno you didn't see any. Why?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: You can see from the report that on the 16th, we were in Travnik. Then on the 17th, a dispatch arrived saying that the prisoners had not been transferred to Zenica because the vehicles were faulty, and we went up there to see what the true reason was, because these prisoners were not transferred to the POW camp in Zenica, because we believed that the conditions to hold them would be better there. They were closer to us for the monitoring -- for purposes of monitoring and for their security. We left Travnik quite late --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... you didn't have the time. But when Mr. Handzic told you that there was a problem, two soldiers were beaten, one of them died as a result, didn't you then feel it necessary to examine this incident more closely by going to see the detainees? You knew that your report would be forwarded to the 3rd Corps Commander, and he perhaps might have wanted to know more about the incident, but your men -- your reference is very brief. You mentioned a problem, but in fact one doesn't know anything about what happened. Why didn't you try to deal with this matter more extensively?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Because we would have acquired the same information and then we would again instruct Mr. Handzic to issue charges, which then he would pass on to the military prosecutor's office. And I believe that we would have just doubled the whole work. He told me that he had already spoken to one of Croats who had remained there who was in excellent -- on excellent terms with his neighbours, Bosniaks, and who moved freely around Bugojno. And he never at any point said that -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question: As far as the Iskra stadium is concerned, did you ever visit the stadium to see what the detention conditions were like for the people who were held there? Did you go into the stadium or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: No, because they were just considering that possibility at that time. And according to the order, you could see that the stadium was actually set up on the 28th. I don't remember exactly, but it was after we left Bugojno. On the 24th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 57, line 4, you said that, "We knew what was happening thanks to the communications that had been established." As far as the system of communication is concerned between the place where you were when you were in Zenica and the 3rd Corps and the units in the field, how did you see the problem of communications by radio, in writing, over the phone? Did you feel that there were any communication problems at that level? Were things running smoothly? Could you provide us with some clarification? Because awhile ago you said that, "We knew what was happening." So I would like to know whether the communications functioned properly. Did everything go smoothly? What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I said that we knew as much as we had access to based on the system of dispatches which were arriving at the command. I didn't work in the communications centre, so I cannot talk to you about all the difficulties and how that proceeded because I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the dispatches, did you yourself read them? Were you familiar with these dispatches?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Each dispatch that arrived at the security centre was accessible to all the employees at the security centre to read. So whoever wanted to read it could read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. A few questions I would like to put to you. The first is the -- on the two soldiers who beat up six HVO prisoners. It has never been said explicitly by you or by your report, but I assume that these were soldiers of the 307th Brigade. Is that correct or were they from another unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I think that it does state in the report that the assistant security commander said that it -- that these were his soldiers. So these were members of the 307th Brigade and that he took measures and that he went and had them set free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, your report says in the English translation, "Handzic said he had a problem with two soldiers," but if I may read that as meaning two soldiers of his brigade, then it answers my question. When you told us about your trip to the local security -- assistant security commander's in August, I remember you saying that this was the first time you had the opportunity to do so. Is that -- do I remember that correctly? I'm not sure whether I do.

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Have there been other trips later on to the same local assistant commanders for security having the same purpose or is it also the last trip you made to them?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: That was the first and last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution if they have any questions to put to the witness that arise from the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Defence counsel is always the last to take the floor, and they may ask questions that arise out of the answers the witness provided to the Chamber and I'll give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zlotrg, you said that this was your first and last time that you went to Bugojno. Before you, who used to go to Bugojno after the events that occurred between the army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: I said that it was the chief, Mr. Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who determined who would go and when out in the field to carry out a part of the military security tasks?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Mr. Dugalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, except for you, other members of the military security sector could go out into the field and to other units?

utterances.speaker: EDIB ZLOTRG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this concludes your re-examination. Thank you for your contribution to establishing the truth. You have answered the questions put to you by the Defence counsel, by the Prosecution, with the exception of one question that we did not authorise. You have also answered the questions put to you by the Judges. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you and I wish you a good trip home and all the best in your career as a forensics expert. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now give the floor to the Defence so that we can deal with the documents. There are seven documents. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we propose that the following documents be admitted as Defence exhibits: 1320, 1391, 1392, and that the documents which were marked previously as ID documents, DH63 ID, DH176 ID, and DH62 ID be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And DH1319, 1319?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's been admitted. You are quite right. Are there any objections from the Prosecution? Any objections to admitting these documents into evidence, documents which have been recognised and commented on?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, you may take the floor to provide us with exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These documents will be exhibited -- admitted into evidence. 1320 will be admitted. Its English version will be DH1320/E. DH1391. Its English version DH1391/E. DH1392. The English version of this document will be DH1392/E. The following documents were previously marked for identification and will now be given final exhibit numbers: DH63. The English version of the document will be DH63/E. DH176; the English version will be DH176/E. And finally DH62; the English version will be DH62/E. That concludes the list, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber takes note of these exhibit numbers. As far as the hearing that will be held tomorrow at 9.00 is concerned, we will call the witness who first appeared to appear tomorrow at 9.00. Then the Prosecution will commence with its cross-examination. After that stage, we will have the re-examination, Judges' questions and additional question if necessary. If we finish with this witness in the course of the morning, we will start with the following witness. I'll turn to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is exactly how the Defence thought we would work tomorrow. We will also call Witness Ragib Hodzic. We have already, as I said earlier, informed the Victims and Witnesses Unit that Witness HD will be left for the following week. At the end of the day tomorrow, we will supply the Chamber and the Prosecution with a definite list of witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but it is quite probable that Mr. Hodzic will have to stay until Monday if we don't manage to finish with his examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I requested one hour, and if my learned friends and the Court also had approximately the same number of questions, I believe that we could complete the testimony of Mr. Hodzic tomorrow, because I do not need more than 30 minutes for my examination-in-chief of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence will need 30 minutes for their examination-in-chief of Mr. Hodzic. So you should make your calculations and we will see things more clearly in that case. It is almost 7.00. I will see everyone tomorrow morning at the hearing at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
